turn_text: Welcome into insight for new media broadcasters. I'm Ashley Milis. Today, I have the pleasure of speaking with Congressman Greg Gianforte. He is here discussing the St. Mary Canal failure and a bill in the works that might be changing how the canal repairs are funded. So to begin, do you mind giving our listeners an idea of what's going on right now with the St. Mary Canal failure?

This is a critical piece of infrastructure for years. I've been saying it's probably the most important piece of infrastructure in the state of Montana that needed assistance. And of course, on May 17th, it failed. Drop five along the canal actually washed out. And this means really there's no water along many communities in the highlights. Unfortunately, there's water in the reservoir, the various reservoirs, so we have about 60 days to get it fixed right after it failed. I got on the phone with Secretary of Interior Bernhardt, and he assured me that they would get after it and get it fixed. I have some new news, which is very encouraging. We have a problem with how the project was originally set up. And just this week, in fact, I haven't shared this news anywhere else yet. We have secured a hearing in the U.S. House to change the funding formula so that the federal government will pick up 75% of the maintenance and repair costs. I spoke with the Democrat Chair of the Infrastructure Committee and Natural Resources, and he assured me that we're going to have a hearing on June 24th. So this is coming right up, and this is important to make sure that the money is available to get the St. Mary's project fixed.

turn_text: So what exactly are the details of this new bill?

This is a bill I introduced. The problem was when the project was originally initiated over 100 years ago, the local irrigators were responsible for 75% of the costs and the federal government was responsible for the 25% of the costs. Well, unfortunately, that puts too much of a burden on local irrigators and local communities that depend on this for domestic water and irrigating over 140,000 acres. So what my bill does is changes the funding formula and reverses it so that the federal government picks up 75% of the maintenance and repair costs, whereas the local irrigators and communities only have to pay 25%. And honestly, this just brings it in line with other Bureau of Reclamation irrigation projects across the state and the country.

So I know earlier this week the Milk River Joint Board of Control and the State of Montana Reclamation announced they will be replacing two drop structures on the St. Mary Canal. If this bill is passed, will it apply to these summer repairs?

Well, I think that was a smart move because we have a very short window here to get. They were going to do two this summer anyway. Drop five is the one that failed. So getting after it is very, very important. This is going to apply to these repairs and future repairs. Essentially, this infrastructure, over 100 years old, it is failing and it needs to be replaced. The state has already authorized funds to help match through bonds and now we need to get the federal government to do their part.
